speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The need to fundamentally rethink how we assess and justify the trade-offs between essential development and the preservation of our existing green spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The question is how we move our planning calculus from measuring gross inputs to ensuring net positive outcomes for our environment and our people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Part one: context and scarcity trap as a policy decision.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We support the need for development, but Singaporeans also care deeply about the quality of life, the neighbourhood liveability, the mental well-being afforded by nature and the preservation of mature landscapes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A tension we observe on the ground arises not because of development and preservation are inherently incompatible, but because in practice these two commitments are not weighted equally in our decision making.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For too long, the default notion used to justify redeveloping green spaces we need to develop in land scarce Singapore has been used as a thought terminating cliche.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is factually correct, but it serves to end deliberation rather than begin it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This position was clearly articulated by the then Minister for National Development, Mr Desmond Lee, when addressing similar development trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In his reply to my written Parliamentary Question on the development of Clementi Forest on 4 January 2021, and I quote: "after weighing the alternatives and trade-offs, there will be areas that we cannot avoid developing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nonetheless, for these sites, possible environmental impacts will still be carefully managed, and natural elements will be integrated within developments where possible." While the intent to manage impacts is welcome, my Motion questions the starting premise, whether this insistence on development is truly unavoidable, or if our current framework has a structural tilt that forces the conclusion of no choice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: No choice too early in the process, sometimes before assessment can be done for a fully informed deliberation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Likewise, once a land is zoned B2 Industrial, rightly or wrongly, should the Ministry of National Development (MND) or the Urban Redevelopment Authority accept that it will always be irreversible, even if there is rich biodiversity from 10 to 20 years, 25 years or more of forestation, including the existence of vulnerable birds?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is shaped not only by geography, but by a series of long-standing planning assumptions that I would urge the Government to revisit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When green spaces, whether greenfield or brownfield sites are presented as inevitable sacrifices, we must ask, have we genuinely exhausted all options to better rationalise existing cleared land?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Have we truly intensified underutilised spaces, gone underground or rethink land intensive systems before concluding that forest must once again bear the cost?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The issue, therefore, is not whether Singapore should develop, but whether our decision frameworks adequately account for what we lose.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ask whether our structures truly account for the cumulative long-term and irreversible losses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They are the inevitable consequence of endless densification.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Part two: the Serangoon River Forest, a case study of policy failure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Works to develop a bus depot in the middle of the part of the forest between Tampines Road and Buangkok East Drive began a few months ago to the chagrin of my residents living less than 200 metres away, including residents at Kingsford Waterbay Condominium.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have been engaged by my residents and many others in Hougang, who highlight this area's role as a last green lung in their vicinity, indeed in the east of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Their concerns have also been reflected in media coverage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This classification appears to rest on the historical use of the surrounding area stretching up to Lorong Halus, which included two kampungs, agricultural, sewage and landfill activities before the land naturally reforested over the last 10 to 25 years between Tampines Road and Pasir Ris Industrial Drive 1.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A brownfield destination prioritises the past commercial zoning over the present ecological function.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It allows the Government to look at a 10- to 25-year forest and call it scrubland, simply because it was historically a developed site.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we are committed to regreening Singapore, we must acknowledge that natural rewilding is a success story, not a planning inconvenience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we encounter brownfield sites where natural rewilding has occurred, could we assess them not solely by what they were, or even what they are at this moment, but by what they are demonstrably becoming?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This absence of data means the decision to clear is made in an information vacuum, relying on decades old zoning, rather than current, verifiable ecological reality.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The question is not whether such sites meet a narrow threshold of environmental significance today, but whether they are on a clear ecological trajectory that, if allowed to continue, will support meaningful biodiversity over the next 10, 15 or 20 years or more.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A second policy question is whether all planning assumptions have been revisited to site the bus depot on existing developments in the area instead of the developing on new space.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is not an issue pertinent to Lorong Halus Bus Depot alone, but for all pending development on green spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are there unpopular but critical planning choices we could make to preserve the little greenery we have left?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is there a symmetry in our planning outcomes where some land users consume a disproportionate share of land relative to the households they serve, yet are rarely subjected to scrutiny with green spaces bearing the cost?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These figures are not cited to argue against roads or transport or any form of infrastructure development, which are clearly essential.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Rather, they illustrate an asymmetry in how land use trade-offs are examined.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When housing, transport or other established systems require land, their footprints are often treated as given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When green spaces are involved, however, the conclusion that I must give away is often treated as the more convenient choice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we defer the hard task of rationalising land hungry systems today, we effectively pass the burden of rationalisation to future generations, while simultaneously depriving them of the very green spaces that could have provided environmental resilience, cooling and liveability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, in other words, future Singaporeans will inherit the same land intensive system, but with even less natural capital left to work with.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we clear a mature green space and replace it with hard permanent infrastructure, we lock in a particular development pathway, often for decades, sometimes permanently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Built infrastructure can be more easily and quickly adapted, intensified or removed as needs change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we clear an established forest or green corridor, the loss is immediate, but recovery is slow.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The cooling effect, ecological function and the biodiversity that took decades to develop cannot simply be reconstructed on demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even with replanting, it may take many years of equivalent functional value to return.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we face rising temperatures, more intense rainfall and increased urban stress, the ability to redeploy land for cooling, absorption or ecological buffering becomes more valuable, not less.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Decisions that permanently eliminate these possibilities should therefore be subject to especially careful scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A more balanced decision framework would explicitly ask, does the development lock us into a path that cannot easily be undone?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, is that loss of flexibility justified by truly exceptional public benefit?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Part three: the true cost of loss, functional value and irreversibility.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But this target, while laudable, obscures the net loss when mature greenery is cleared, especially when the decision is not informed by an EIA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Serangoon River Forest is not just a collection of trees.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is a vital part of the climate control system for this part of the northeast of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Studies showed a pronounced urban island effect in densely built areas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mature-dense canopies provide the most effective passive solution to shade and cooling through evapotranspiration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By removing this forest, we are imposing an immediate permanent environmental cost on the surrounding Hougang, Sengkang, Punggol, Tampines and Pasir Ris residents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Higher ambient temperatures reduce shade and degraded thermal comfort.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Ecological science tells us that green spaces function as systems, not isolated plots.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clearing these mature land risks fragmentations of a key corridor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is a bigger stretch of green spaces on the eastern half of Singapore, from Tampines Road to Pasir Ris Industrial Drive 1.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond nature, further development would result in residents in Hougang, Sengkang, Punggol and elsewhere in north-east losing a space that provides a unique sense of wellbeing and community life, an intangible asset that no number on a balance sheet can capture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The building and a bus depot are sadly the first step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Water absorption studies conducted by the Nanyang Technological University in 2021 showed that forested areas provide a critical sponge effect, intercepting rainfall and regulating run-off.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the increasing unpredictability of rainfall and the greater incidence of ponding, removing this function, especially near a river, is a decision that must be weighed with the utmost care against potential flood risk.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Economic valuation confirms that preserving the Serangoon Forest provides superior welfare for residents using the park connector all the way to Punggol.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we evaluate mitigation, we must factor in time and irreversibility.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If a functional loss is permanent or requires a recovery period of say, five, 10 or 20 years, it must face a substantially higher justification threshold than a minor reversible inconvenience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, part four: a new framework – net outcomes and functional value.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To address this structural tilt and prevent further decisions based on historical zoning instead of current functional value, we need a balanced decision framework that explicitly values what we preserve.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I propose the following elements for a revised planning and assessment framework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must measure the net change in unfragmented canopy cover, cooling effect and ecological function.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must factor in the time to replacement when evaluating mitigation, acknowledging the ecological premium of mature established greenery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must prioritise green spaces by what they do in a regional context.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As the Government plans the massive new Housing and Development Board (HDB) town at the Paya Lebar Air Base site, it must recognise that large parts of the limited existing green spaces within and on the eastern fringe of the air base will be developed or severely affected by the construction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These air base green spaces may be smaller or have less ecological merit than the current Serangoon River Forest, stretching from Tampines Road to Serangoon East Dam and Coney Island.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It would make far greater ecological and planning sense to preserve and utilise the current well developed Serangoon River Forest as an established green belt to mitigate against the heat impact from the future big new town.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is strategically superior to relying on artificially-created neighbourhood parks or park connectors at the air base site.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Agencies must clearly demonstrate that avoidance and minimisation were explored before mitigation is proposed, specifically when my residents appealed to the Land Transport Authority (LTA) or MND for the bus depot site to be shifted to the current heavy vehicle park along Tampines Road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Apply a higher justification threshold to any decision that results in an irreversible loss or requires a recovery period.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must evaluate impacts in the neighbourhood or corridor level, not project by project.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Multiple compliant decisions when accumulated over time in a small area can still lead to a degraded, less liveable environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When trade-offs are made, we must clearly state what is gained and what is lost in clean terms, ensuring that the environmental cost do not disproportionately fall on the immediate neighbours, while the benefits are distributed citywide.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They should also be actively communicated to stakeholders early on, rather than leaving it to consultation exercise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must hold planning decisions across all existing land uses to the same level of scrutiny as green spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When development is proposed on vegetated land, we must ask whether existing land hungry system have been reviewed, intensified, co-located or rationalised to avoid further loss of natural capital.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we allow the label of brownfield to exempt us from doing a basic baseline biodiversity study on EIA on a mature self-reforested site, and if we fail to see the strategic value of this established green lung in the face of major future regional development, like the Paya Lebar Air Base Town, we risk making decisions that are blind to current ecological reality and future climate needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge MND and all planning agencies to review their decision framework to ensure that our decisions are based on net outcomes, functional value and long-term resilience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What we choose to preserve today is what will define Singapore's livability tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I wanted to say that our objectives are the same.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our objectives to balance different land use are the same, but we have different views on this, and I disagree with how he has characterised the approach we have been taking all these years, and it is fine to have these different views.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But let me architect and let me frame how we look at land use planning.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In recent years, for example, as Members of this House know, and we have debated.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singaporeans' demand for housing has grown and the Government has, therefore, ramped up public and private housing supply in the past few years, and we will continue keeping up a steady housing supply if demand remains strong.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And to meet Singaporeans needs, we must maximise how we use our limited land.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, we are redeveloping brownfield sites, such as golf courses, industrial areas, and also activating underused spaces, such as via ducts and carpark rooftops.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are also building higher where possible, and the relaxation of aviation height limits near airports will open new possibilities for future intensification while maintaining liveable spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As the Member alluded to, we are also exploring the use of more underground spaces to free up surface land for more liveable uses, including at Gali Batu and this builds on earlier efforts, such as the Jurong Rock Caverns and the deep tunnel sewerage system.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we are already looking down, we are already looking up.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And through our North-South corridor project, we are also diverting vehicular traffic underground to free up more ground level space for cycling, walking, green spaces and other spaces that Singaporeans enjoy.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At the same time, we are also co-locating suitable uses within integrated developments to optimise our land use, while also bringing convenience to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This includes our Tampines Hub and Bukit Canberra as well as upcoming integrated community hubs in Siglap and Toa Payoh.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These hubs will bring together sports facilities, healthcare, community spaces in one convenient location – all things which Singaporeans want.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But even as we do our best to optimise existing build up areas, we will still need to strike that balance between development and conserving and preserving our green spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have also identified key ecological corridors between core habitats.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have established nature park networks and nature corridors along these corridors, such as the Labrador Nature Park Network and the Clementi Nature Corridor, that is alongside them.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And the National Parks Board's ecological profiling exercise also guides our conservation strategies, including to sensitively integrate nature into our urban landscape upfront within our land use plans.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also ensure our green spaces are accessible and near homes.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Because of these efforts, in fact, we are recognised.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singapore today is recognised as one of the world's greenest cities.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Green View Index shows that we are in fact ahead of most cities in our provision of urban tree coverage, including those with lower population densities.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have in place supporting efforts that allow us to contribute more effectively to enhance green cover, biodiversity and ecological connectivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But to achieve all this, we adopt a robust systematic and science-based framework to balance developmental needs and conserving our green spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We rigorously study the trade-offs and alternatives and consult stakeholders where relevant.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Under our EIA Framework, we start by consulting technical agencies on the sites' potential ecological and biodiversity value.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And if there is potentially significant environmental impact from the development, we require an EIA study to assess in greater detail – the nature and the magnitude of the impact and to develop more mitigating measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And based on the EIA findings, agencies will then carefully consider the extent of the potential impact and the adequacy of the proposed mitigation measures in consultation with nature groups and community stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These stakeholders' expertise and feedback inform the mitigation recommendations in the EIA.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We then make the environmental study reports publicly available online so that the public can provide feedback, and this is our default practice unless there are national security concerns where confidentiality is required.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, I wanted to correct the mischaracterisation of the Member when he said that no EIA is needed as it is brownfield and zone B2.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In fact, I just mentioned that it is not true that brownfield sites automatically do not require EIA.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On his specific point about Serangoon Forest, he spoke about the east of Sungai Serangoon and Serangoon Forest, and I previously explained in Parliament in November that this area has been zoned for industrial use since 1998.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Member Gerald Giam was informed of the rezoning and gave no comments.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The site is intended to be progressively developed to help us to achieve a few objectives.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, there is value and benefit to residents living in the area.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The area was previously a municipal waste landfill known as the Tampines Tipping Ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Technical agencies have assessed that this site is not a sensitive nature area and the environmental impact of the bus depot is limited.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The vegetation on the site is a result of regeneration of the last 10 to 15 years, comprising young exotic dominated secondary forests, scrubland, grassland and ponds.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These habitats are commonly found in cleared or disturbed areas and generally have lower ecological value than more mature forest habitats such as native dominated secondary forests.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This includes hoarding the work site, which also serves to prevent wildlife vehicular collisions, and conducting checks for birds' nests and other wildlife before site clearance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister of State, you have about a minute left.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I know it matters to all of you.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It matters because we all want our green spaces, we all want our homes, our hospitals, our schools, our jobs, our workspaces and transport facilities to get us around.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I wish we have an abundance of land and space to do all that without trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We build upwards and downwards and constantly repurpose our land for evolving uses.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At the same time, it is our responsibility to be upfront about we can do and what we cannot do.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We must mitigate impact where we can and make adjustments where possible.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But ultimately, we must take a view and make a decision.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These decisions will continue to confront us as we build our city in nature and provide homes and jobs to Singaporeans – just as it has confronted our predecessors.
